title: P99 fanout collapse case study: end-to-end profiling and mitigations
content:
Summary:
We observed a sustained p99 latency regression for long-tail requests on the hosted inference route /v1/generate (model: rwf-13b). p50/p95 remained near baseline but p99 increased ~3.2x for a ~2-hour window (2025-11-07T02:10–04:30 UTC). Customer-facing errors were minimal, but internal SLA alerts fired and a canary rollback was initiated.

Scope / impact:
- Route: /v1/generate (default tenant pool)
- Traffic spike: +18% QPS vs baseline during incident window due to retargeted marketing traffic
- Affected quantile: p99 primarily, p95 marginally elevated for some cohorts, p50 unchanged
- Observed symptoms: long tail traces dominated by one or two stages; high variance in per-batch wait time; increased retry counts on a small fraction of requests.

High-level hypothesis (short):
A combination of synchronized KV-cache TTL expirations and transient fanout to remote KV store created intermittent long-latency fetches. Those fetches lengthened the batcher wait window and caused head-of-line blocking for other co-located requests, producing p99 tail events.

Data collected / artifacts used:
- Sampled traces (10k traces sampled with 1:200 deterministic sampler) tagged by model + tenant
- Per-stage histograms (ingress, tokenize, kv-lookup, batch-wait, forward, emit, egress) across p50/p95/p99
- Node-level metrics (CPU steal, runqueue length, net I/O)
- Batcher queue depth and cohort-size time series
- KV store latency heatmap (remote store + redis cache miss patterns)
- Relevant dashboards: https://grafana.redwood.company/d/abcd123/e2e-latency

Representative per-stage quantiles (aggregated across impacted traces) — values in ms:
- Ingress (parse/validate headers): p50=2, p95=5, p99=15
- Tokenize: p50=1, p95=4, p99=12
- KV cache lookup (local memcached): p50=3, p95=25, p99=540
- Remote KV fetch (when local miss, background call to remote store): p50=20, p95=80, p99=920  <-- present only on miss traces
- Batcher wait (time waiting for batching/coalescing): p50=6, p95=60, p99=880
- Forward compute (GPU): p50=48, p95=130, p99=670
- Emit/handoff (serialize + socket write): p50=6, p95=18, p99=210
- Egress/response write: p50=2, p95=7, p99=25

Notes: p99 numbers are dominated by two cases: (A) KV local-cache miss followed by slow remote fetch; (B) microburst where many concurrent requests queued and batcher delayed until one slow token path finished. The remote KV fetch and batcher wait are strongly correlated (pearson r=0.67 for p99 traces).

Trace archetype (synthesized p99):
- 0ms: request ingress
- 5ms: tokenize finishes
- 8ms: local KV lookup -> miss, async fetch started
- 15ms: request enters batcher; batcher holds for coalescing (waiting for other in-flight requests)
- 200–900ms: remote KV single-call takes 0.6–0.9s (tail event) -> returns; request now proceeds
- 920ms: forward queued on GPU, actual compute 600ms (on the tail path we saw GPU preemption in 3/15 traces)
- 1530ms: emit + egress -> response (total ~1.5s)

Key findings and evidence:
1) Synchronized TTL expirations: cluster-wide key churn caused many tenants to experience cache misses simultaneously. Inspecting cache TTL histograms shows microbursts at epoch-aligned intervals (cron-ish churn from background job that invalidates semantics keys every 60s). Evidence: spike in miss ratio aligned to job start times.
2) Remote KV tail: when local miss occurs, we synchronously call a remote store that has higher tail latency under modest concurrency. These calls are currently synchronous in the request path and block the batcher slot. Traces show remote fetch latency correlates tightly with batcher wait increases.
3) Batcher semantics + head-of-line: batcher waits for a quorum (~N requests or timeout). A single request delayed by remote fetch holds the batch open and increases wait for others. Our current batcher doesn't preempt or evict long-wait requests; no per-request priority.
4) CPU / IO contention on some hosts: node telemetry shows increased runqueue lengths and small CPU steals coincident with tail traces. This exacerbates forward pass scheduling and increases p99 further.
5) Unstaggered background tasks: a background TTL refresher ran on many replicas without jitter, producing synchronized cache invalidations.

Rejected hypotheses (quick):
- Model sharding overload: evidence against — GPU queue/throughput steady except for minority of traces.
- Network partitioning: no sustained packet loss or route flaps in infra logs.

Experiments / repro attempts performed:
- Localized replay with synthetic trace driver: replayed 1k concurrent requests with injected remote KV tail; reproduced p99 increase when KV miss rate > 4%.
- TTL jitter deployment (stagger background job by random jitter): immediate reduction in synchronous miss bursts in canary cluster.
- Batcher timeout tuning: reduced batcher max wait from 25ms -> 10ms in canary; p99 for small requests improved, but throughput dropped ~3%.
- Async remote fetch proof-of-concept: offloaded remote KV fetch from critical batch path and returned cached default; visible p99 reduction but requires correctness checks for semantics where KV value affects model output.

Mitigations (short-term / tactical):
- Deploy jitter to background TTL refresher across replicas (owner: Maya, due: 2025-11-12)
- Increase KV local cache size on hotspots + short-term TTL increase to reduce synchronized misses (owner: Ethan, due: 2025-11-14)
- Shorten batcher max wait for interactive routes to 10ms for canary traffic (owner: Ravi, due: 2025-11-13)
- Add tracing flag kv_hit=true/false to sampled traces to make filterable dashboards (owner: Sofia, due: 2025-11-10)

Mitigations (mid-term / strategic):
- Async-fetch/pledge flow: return quickly with a "stale-ok" value or partial output and attach an async update when remote KV resolved; requires product decision for semantics (owner: eng-arch, due: 2026-01-15)
- Batcher redesign: support per-request priority and fast-path for singletons to avoid head-of-line blocking (owner: batcher-team, RFC in GH PR #842)
- Backpressure-resilient remote store: introduce client-side hedging (duplicate slow calls) and circuit-breakers for remote KV; coordinate with infra team on capacity (owner: infra, due: 2026-02-01)

Observability recommendations (short list):
- Add per-stage p50/p95/p99 histograms with kv_hit dimension on the main dashboard.
- Correlate batcher queue depth with kv_miss boolean in traces.
- Add synthetic test that simulates a rolling TTL invalidation with controlled jitter to catch synchronized misses in CI.
- Alerting: create alert when kv_miss_rate > 2% and p99_batch_wait > 200ms for > 5m.

Decision log and next steps (proposed):
- Immediate: deploy TTL jitter and trace flag to canary. Monitor for 24h (owner: Maya + Sofia).
- Short: tune batcher wait for interactive route rollouts behind config flag and measure throughput vs p99 tradeoff (owner: Ravi).
- Medium: converge on async-fetch design or stale-serve semantics with product; start RFC and security review for data correctness (owner: eng-arch).

Open questions / risks:
- Stale-serve semantics may change customer outputs; do we accept transient staleness for latency? Which customers must opt-out?
- Hedging remote calls increases load on remote store—need capacity plan.
- Batcher timeout reduction reduces token throughput; how to balance cost vs latency?

Appendix: quick primers / how to repro locally
1) Repro harness outline: run the trace-replay driver against a canary gateway with synthetic TTL-invalidation job that fires every 60s, then add jitter and compare p99.
2) Useful queries: trace search: tag:model=rwf-13b AND kv_hit=false AND duration>800ms; dashboard: e2e-latency-by-stage p99 panel.
3) Logs to check: node /proc metrics, redis client slowlog, batcher queue telemetry.

Notes to reviewer: this doc is a working case study intended to capture the incident, quick wins, and prioritized engineering work. Many mitigations are already instrumented in canary. Please comment on the async-fetch semantics and whether product will accept a stale-first flow for interactive routes.

Acknowledgments: thanks to Maya for the cache telemetry deep dive, Ethan for the remote-store profiling, and Sofia for the tracing instrumentation.

-- end of notes --
